articles.title: Sharjah Dry Ports reports record TEUs in a single month
articles.summary: Gulftainer has rebranded its flagship inland facility in Sajaa as Sharjah Dry Ports (SDP), a name that reflects the site’s wider role as a gateway for the Northern Emirates. articles.body: Gulftainer has rebranded its flagship inland facility in Sajaa as Sharjah Dry Ports (SDP), a name that reflects the site’s wider role as a gateway for the Northern Emirates. The facility serves manufacturing zones, distribution hubs and regional trade corridors, with last-mile connections to Sharjah, Khorfakkan Port and beyond. The announcement coincides with a record: SDP handled 150,000 TEUs in a single month, the highest monthly throughput in its history. The site covers 70 hectares and lies about 90 kilometres from Khorfakkan Port. It has a fully interlocked yard of 50,000 square metres, 5,000 square metres of modern warehousing and 30,000 square metres of bulk and container storage. It has direct road links to all major UAE ports, with rail connectivity planned for the future. Launched in December 2025 as Gulftainer’s second bonded dry port, it offers bonded storage, cold chain solutions and access to manufacturing hubs, and is designed to help customers move cargo more efficiently with shorter turnaround times. Omar Rishi, Global Chief Commercial Officer at Gulftainer, said the record shows the resilience, efficiency and scale of the group’s integrated logistics ecosystem. He described the change from Sajaa to Sharjah Dry Ports as reflecting a commitment to building the future of trade, with inland and maritime gateways working as one to bring cargo closer to the customer more quickly.

articles.title: COSCO unveils massive supertanker fleet push
articles.summary: Chinese tanker giant COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation has unveiled a sweeping fleet expansion involving 24 VLCC newbuildings, signing contracts worth RMB9.48bn ($1.42bn) for ten supertankers and lining up another 14 through long-term bareboat charters. The Shanghai- and Hong Kong-listed owner disclosed the deals...
articles.body: Finance and Insurance Greater China Shipyards Tankers COSCO unveils massive supertanker fleet push Adis Ajdin November 9, 2026 0 0 3 minutes read Panjin Municipality Panjin Municipality Chinese tanker giant COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation has unveiled a sweeping fleet expansion involving 24 VLCC newbuildings, signing contracts worth RMB9.48bn ($1.42bn) for ten supertankers and lining up another 14 through long-term bareboat charters. The Shanghai- and Hong Kong-listed owner disclosed the deals on November 9, with its wholly owned subsidiary Hainan Cosco Shipping Energy Transportation placing orders at two Chinese shipyards. Six VLCCs have been contracted at Yangzhou COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry for RMB5.69bn ($853m), while Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Corporation (DSIC) has secured four vessels worth RMB3.79bn ($569m). The contracts are priced at approximately RMB948m ($142m) per ship, with the Yangzhou series scheduled for delivery between August 2029 and November 2030. The four DSIC vessels are due between September 2029 and May 2030. The Yangzhou newbuildings will feature LNG-ready fuel systems, while the DSIC quartet will be designed for future conversion to LNG or methanol dual-fuel propulsion. The Yangzhou deal is classified as a related-party transaction because the shipyard belongs to the COSCO group and still requires shareholder approval. The DSIC contract has received board approval without requiring a further shareholder vote. Alongside the direct newbuilding investment, COSCO Shipping Energy has approved plans to take another 14 VLCC newbuildings on bareboat charter from six Chinese financial leasing companies. The programme, handled through subsidiary Huanyu Shipowning, carries maximum rental commitments of RMB17.4bn ($2.61bn) over charter periods of up to 20 years. Bank of Communications Financial Leasing will provide four LNG dual-fuel VLCCs, while ICBC Financial Leasing will supply three. Agricultural Bank of China Financial Leasing is lined up for three conventionally powered vessels, with Bank of China Financial Leasing providing another one.CITIC Financial Leasing will contribute two LNG dual-fuel vessels, while Minsheng Financial Leasing will provide the remaining ship. The charter programme comprises ten LNG dual-fuel and four conventionally powered VLCCs, with all 14 vessels expected to enter service during 2030. The leasing arrangements still require shareholder approval, with the company opting for the bareboat structure to expand its operating fleet while limiting upfront capital expenditure. Taken together, the announcements cover ten directly ordered VLCCs and another 14 planned chartered newbuildings, marking a major expansion of Cosco Shipping Energy’s crude tanker fleet heading into the next decade. Separately, the company’s board has approved another proposal involving long-term leasing and financing arrangements for 16 VLCC newbuildings. The related-party proposal, which also requires shareholder approval, has yet to be accompanied by details of financing partners, shipyards, contract values or delivery schedules. The company said further information would be disclosed once specific agreements are signed, leaving it unclear whether the 16 vessels represent additional fleet expansion or overlap with other newbuilding plans. The proposed charters will run for up to 20 years, with the ships scheduled to enter the fleet during 2030.The largest allocation is four LNG dual-fuel VLCCs from Bank of Communications Financial Leasing, carrying a maximum combined rental commitment of RMB5.2bn ($779m). ICBC Financial Leasing will provide three LNG dual-fuel vessels, Agricultural Bank of China Financial Leasing three conventionally powered VLCCs, and Bank of China Financial Leasing one conventional vessel. CITIC Financial Leasing is lined up for two LNG dual-fuel ships, with Minsheng Financial Leasing providing another one. The arrangement covers ten LNG dual-fuel vessels and four conventionally powered VLCCs, although the broader specifications also refer to fuel-ready technologies. Cosco Shipping Energy said the bareboat structure would allow it to expand its fleet without the same level of upfront capital expenditure required for direct ship ownership. The programme was approved by the company’s board on November 9 but still requires shareholder approval because its cumulative leasing transactions over the previous 12 months exceed 50% of audited net assets. The announcement came alongside the company’s separate RMB9.48bn investment in ten owned VLCC newbuildings at Yangzhou Cosco Shipping Heavy Industry and Dalian Shipbuilding Industry, taking the group’s newly announced potential fleet additions to 24 supertankers. articles.title: Snowbird Technologies Demonstrates On-Demand Hybrid Manufacturing at RIMPAC 2026
articles.summary: Snowbird Technologies, a U.S. manufacturer of mission-critical equipment and deployable manufacturing systems, announced successful operational results from the company's participation in NPS CAMRE's Littoral and Expeditionary Advanced Manufacturing and Repair Experiment at RIMPAC 2026…
articles.body: Snowbird Technologies Demonstrates On-Demand Hybrid Manufacturing at RIMPAC 2026 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 9, 2026 © Snowbird Technologies Snowbird Technologies, a U.S. manufacturer of mission-critical equipment and deployable manufacturing systems, announced successful operational results from the company's participation in NPS CAMRE's Littoral and Expeditionary Advanced Manufacturing and Repair Experiment at RIMPAC 2026, where its SAMM Tech deployable hybrid manufacturing platform demonstrated on-demand metal additive manufacturing both aboard the USS Essex and ashore at Schofield Barracks, Hawaii. Operating as part of the Naval Postgraduate School's Consortium for Advanced Manufacturing Research & Education (CAMRE) and FLEETWERX initiatives, SAMM Tech successfully produced mission-critical components using the wire-laser metal additive manufacturing industrial solution Meltio Engine Blue and nitrogen as the process gas, first aboard the USS Essex and subsequently at Leader's Field at Schofield Barracks using nitrogen supplied by an on-site generator. The deployment demonstrated the ability to manufacture replacement parts closer to the point of need while reducing reliance on traditional procurement and extended supply chains. During the exercise, SAMM Tech produced seven parts, including oxygen tank brackets, drain caps, load test clamp components, turnbuckles, a 4-inch pipe flange, and an air pressure radio six-pack. According to Snowbird's RIMPAC results analysis, four of the seven parts delivered cost advantages compared with OEM procurement, with reported savings of up to 351%: Oxygen Tank Brackets (Qty 12): Printed in an estimated 75 hours for approximately $2,492 in wire and gas, compared with estimated OEM procurement costs of $9,624 from PHNSY and $10,224 to USS Essex. ﻿﻿Load Test Clamp Outer: Printed in approximately 3 hours for $101, compared with $420 from PHNSY and $455 to USS Essex - representing 351% reported savings. ﻿﻿Load Test Clamp Inner: Printed in approximately 9 hours for $289, compared with $420 from PHNSY and $455 to USS Essex. ﻿﻿Air Pressure Radio (6-pack): Printed in approximately 5 hours for $154, compared with $624 from PHNSY and $654 to USS Essex - representing 325% reported savings. The results also demonstrated the value of manufacturing parts on demand when conventional procurement may require longer lead times. Snowbird's analysis notes that even when additive manufacturing costs exceeded procurement costs for an individual part, on-demand production can avoid weeks of supply delay and support mission readiness. For example, approximately 692 hours of procurement time on one part order were avoided using SAMM Tech on location during the exercise. For the complete RIMPAC 2026 results, including part-level print times, manufacturing costs and procurement comparisons, see Snowbird Technologies' accompanying sheet, " RIMPAC 2026 Results: Deploy. Print. Sustain. "

articles.title: Optics11 Receives Additional $55m Investment to Meet Global Security Infrastructure Demands
articles.summary: Optics11 announced it has secured USD$55.9 million (€50 million) in follow-on equity investment to accelerate its capacity to meet global customer demand. As European governments and defense organizations scramble to rebuild effective security infrastructure…
articles.body: Optics11 Receives Additional $55m Investment to Meet Global Security Infrastructure Demands Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 9, 2026 ASWINABO. © Optics11 Optics11 announced it has secured USD$55.9 million (€50 million) in follow-on equity investment to accelerate its capacity to meet global customer demand. As European governments and defense organizations scramble to rebuild effective security infrastructure, this equity round takes total investment in the Company to more than USD$111.9 million (€100 million) in just 15 months. The latest round is backed by existing institutional investors SET Ventures, FORWARD.one, Value Creation Capital and JOIN Capital, with all four reinvesting as Optics11 enters its next phase of international growth. The new capital will support increased manufacturing and international expansion, enabling the Company to respond to growing global demand, expand its operational capabilities and deliver its technology to an increasing number of customers and partners. The investment represents a milestone for Optics11, reflecting both the growing commercial opportunity for its technology and the speed at which the security environment surrounding critical infrastructure has changed. Governments across the globe are reassessing their ability to protect national infrastructure as hybrid warfare increasingly extends beyond traditional military domains and into the seas, while global electricity networks face growing pressure from electrification, rising energy demand and the need for greater grid resilience. Together, these challenges are creating international demand for advanced sensing technologies capable of protecting the infrastructure upon which modern economies depend. At the heart of Optics11 is the same fiber optic sensing technology first developed from research at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, from which the Company was founded in 2011. By using light to capture minute acoustic signals, rather than powered electronics at the sensing point, the technology remains silent and immune to electromagnetic interference while delivering sensitive, high-quality data. Underwater, OptiBarrier provides persistent seabed sensing capable of detecting and classifying targets at distances of up to 100 kilometers from the shoreline, while OptiArray brings the same fiber optic sensing capability to a mobile towed array for anti-submarine warfare and maritime surveillance. Across energy grids, OptiFinder applies fiber optic acoustic sensing to detect and precisely localize partial discharge within high-voltage assets and is now in live deployment globally. Earlier this year, the Dutch Ministry of Defense selected Optics11's containerized OptiArray technology for its ASWINABO (Anti-Submarine Warfare In A Box) program, enabling advanced underwater sensing capability to be deployed from a much broader range of crewed and uncrewed surface vessels, including civilian ships. The program is intended to strengthen the readiness and self-sufficiency of the Royal Netherlands Navy and represents a validation of Optics11's technology as nations across the globe look to rapidly increase maritime surveillance capabilities.

articles.title: Lloyd’s Register and MAWANI sign agreement on Saudi port development
articles.summary: Lloyd’s Register (LR) and the Saudi Ports Authority (MAWANI) have signed a three-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to support the development of Saudi Arabia’s maritime and port sectors. articles.body: Lloyd’s Register (LR) and the Saudi Ports Authority (MAWANI) have signed a three-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to support the development of Saudi Arabia’s maritime and port sectors. The agreement focuses on port operations, digitalisation, sustainability, safety and professional training. Both organisations will explore opportunities to improve port management and strengthen maritime services across the country. MAWANI President Suliman Al-Mazroua and LR CEO Nick Brown signed the agreement. The partnership also supports Saudi Arabia’s National Transport and Logistics Strategy, which aims to establish the country as a major international logistics hub. Focus on digitalisation and port operations Under the agreement, LR and MAWANI will examine ways to improve port operations and management systems. Their discussions will also cover maritime safety, regulatory compliance and risk management. In addition, the two organisations will explore environmental initiatives, including port decarbonisation and green port programmes. They will assess opportunities to introduce digital solutions and improve the use of data in port operations. Training is another important part of the agreement. Both organisations will consider programmes to develop maritime skills, support local employment and strengthen cooperation between educational institutions and the maritime industry. The agreement builds on an existing partnership between LR and MAWANI. In January 2025, LR secured a contract to support management systems and certification preparations at four Saudi ports. These were Jeddah Islamic Port, King Abdulaziz Port in Dammam, Yanbu Commercial Port and Jubail Commercial Port. The earlier project included work on quality and environmental procedures aligned with ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 standards. It also covered Port State Control processes and personnel training. The new MoU expands the scope of potential cooperation. However, the organisations have not announced specific new projects, investment amounts or implementation dates.

articles.title: Kongsberg Maritime Unveils Arctic Hunter USV
articles.summary: Norwegian maritime technology company Kongsberg Maritime has unveiled the Arctic Hunter USV, a new class of uncrewed surface vessels designed for rapid integration and deployment into Hybrid Fleets.In response to the UK Royal Navy’s development of its hybrid fleet of crewed and uncrewed assets…
articles.body: Kongsberg Maritime Unveils Arctic Hunter USV Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 9, 2026 © Kongsberg Maritime Norwegian maritime technology company Kongsberg Maritime has unveiled the Arctic Hunter USV, a new class of uncrewed surface vessels designed for rapid integration and deployment into Hybrid Fleets. In response to the UK Royal Navy’s development of its hybrid fleet of crewed and uncrewed assets, the Arctic Hunter USV combines commercial ship design with Kongsberg Maritime’s remote and autonomous technologies to deliver anti-submarine warfare (ASW) capability in the High North. Kongsberg Maritime has selected one of its Arctic commercial vessel designs to adapt and optimize for the Royal Navy’s Type 92 ASW requirement. Their uncrewed vessel technology has also already received flag-state approval from classification society DNV and the Norwegian Maritime Authority. The Arctic Hunter USV is designed to be built at pace by commercial shipyards, with military capability integrated by the defense industry. The vessel is equipped with Thales UK’s sovereign submarine-hunting sonar and secure military communications systems. Significant payload capacity and deck space allow the vessel to accommodate alternative or additional mission systems throughout its operational life. Operating from a forward support base inside the Arctic Circle, the Arctic Hunter USV is designed to provide a persistent sensing capability to augment the existing multi-asset ASW infrastructure in the High North. To support accelerated delivery, Kongsberg Maritime is working with its established long-term shipbuilding partner Balaena Maritime, with new ships planned to be delivered from their Birkenhead yard, ready for militarization and operational deployment by the end of this decade. A Type 92 ASW program based upon Arctic Hunter USV supports the Lunna House agreement for the UK and Norway to lead NATO’s adoption of autonomous systems in the High North. Kongsberg Maritime will sign Technology Collaboration Agreements with Thales UK and Balaena Maritime during Atlantic Future Forum this week. These agreements will further strengthen UK and Norway industrial collaboration and support skilled jobs.

articles.body: Asia Containers RCL adds $213m boxship pair to growing orderbook Adis Ajdin November 9, 2026 0 79 1 minute read RCL RCL Thailand’s Regional Container Lines (RCL) has added another two neo-panamax containerships to its expanding newbuilding programme, committing around $213m for a pair of 9,200 teu vessels. The Bangkok-listed carrier has lined up the ships for delivery in 2030 and 2031, with the contract valued at approximately $106.5m per vessel. The shipyard behind the latest order has not been identified. RCL confirmed the newbuildings in its third-quarter financial update, revealing that it had contracted a total of 12 ships during the period.Alongside the 9,200 teu pair, the company listed orders for four 1,900 teu vessels and six 3,100 teu units, with the new tonnage scheduled to enter service from 2028 onwards. The latest deal extends an aggressive fleet expansion programme that has seen RCL return repeatedly to Chinese shipbuilders while also moving into larger vessel classes. In September, the carrier signed for four 3,100 teu ships at CSSC Huangpu Wenchong, taking its programme at the Guangzhou yard to 16 vessels across three designs. That deal followed an order for four 1,900 teu feeders in August. RCL also turned to South Korea’s HD Hyundai Heavy Industries last November for two 14,000 teu ships in a KRW435.3bn ($299m) contract, marking its first newbuilding agreement with the yard. The latest investment comes against a stronger freight market for RCL. Its average freight rate climbed to $624 per teu in the third quarter from $552 in the preceding three months, despite a 4.1% drop in cargo volumes. According to the company, the first six months of measurements from the wave buoy campaign at its commercial site show slightly higher significant wave heights (Hs) and slightly shorter energy periods (Te) than estimated in the simulated dataset from Copernicus. Using these measured conditions in the performance calculations increases the system’s projected power output by up to 20% compared with estimates based on the Copernicus data. With the support of the Danish Foreign Ministry, Wavepiston reported it was also analyzing the market potential of three additional export markets , with the potential to expand the focus next year. Furthermore, Glosten and Wavepiston have been selected through the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Testing Expertise and Access for Marine Energy Research (TEAMER) program to advance wave energy technology. Glosten will evaluate how the assembly, logistics, and installation of the Wavepiston system can be optimized, with the aim of establishing operational guidelines that support Wavepiston’s next full-scale deployment. articles.summary: Heerema Marine Contractors has extended its global framework agreement with Fugro for another four years, securing continued survey and positioning support for its heavy-lift vessel fleet across offshore installation, decommissioning and wind…
articles.body: Fugro Secures Four-Year Extension for Heerema's Heavy-Lift Fleet Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 9, 2026 (Credit: Fugro) Heerema Marine Contractors has extended its global framework agreement with Fugro for another four years, securing continued survey and positioning support for its heavy-lift vessel fleet across offshore installation, decommissioning and wind projects. The renewed agreement runs from January 2027 through December 2030 and covers Fugro's positioning and survey services for Heerema's offshore operations worldwide. Fugro will provide Geo-data and positioning support for the transport, installation and removal of offshore structures, including oil and gas platforms and offshore wind foundations. The services will help Heerema monitor vessel positioning, asset movements and installation progress during offshore campaigns involving large construction vessels. Under the extended agreement, Fugro will also use technologies such as remote operations to support Heerema's projects, drawing on its global network of remote operations centres. The technology enables real-time oversight of offshore activities, with the aim of improving operational efficiency, safety and flexibility. "Over the past four years, we have built a strong working relationship with Heerema and developed a deep understanding of their operational requirements. "This framework extension creates further opportunities for closer collaboration on technology and innovation that support increasingly complex offshore campaigns,” said Thijs Prins, Fugro's Service Line Director Marine Asset Integrity. The four-year extension continues the companies' collaboration on offshore survey and positioning services for Heerema's heavy-lift operations.

articles.body: Greater China Offshore Sinopec awards offshore platform and pipeline contract in China Bojan Lepic November 9, 2026 0 244 1 minute read Chinese energy giant Sinopec has awarded an engineering, procurement and construction contract for the Weizhou oilfield expansion in the Beibu Gulf, involving a new offshore processing platform, subsea pipelines, and fibre-optic cables. The contract was awarded to a consortium comprising Sinopec Petroleum Engineering Design and Sinopec Shengli Oil Construction. The package covers detailed engineering, procurement and fabrication of a new offshore oil and gas processing platform featuring an eight-legged jacket, steel piles, topsides, accommodation facilities, and a well-workover module. The contractors will also install subsea pipelines and communications cables offshore, including riser connections, expansion bends, offshore commissioning, and start-up support. The original tender estimated the package at RMB1.04bn ($146m), although the final contract value has not been disclosed. The project forms part of Sinopec’s development of new production capacity at the Weizhou field, including a new WZ-CEP central processing platform linked to the existing WZ11-4 CEPD installation. The development involves approximately 26 km of subsea pipeline and a parallel fibre-optic cable of similar length. The new platform is designed to accommodate 28 wells, with 16 wells included in the initial drilling programme. These comprise 11 production wells, four water-injection wells, and one gas-injection well. Modifications are also planned for the existing WZ11-4 platform to accommodate the additional production infrastructure. The EPC package has a planned execution period of 615 days, with completion tied to the project’s readiness for first oil. articles.title: Baltic routes, importer shifts and El Niño test grain markets
articles.summary: Black Sea flows remain minimal The Black Sea picture is stark. Vessels sit at anchor offshore, waiting to enter the Danube to load, and the backlog is large. Ukrainian shipments from Izmail and Reni are vital for the export campaign, though volumes are relatively low. Only a few Russian shipments have been observed...
articles.body: Baltic routes, importer shifts and El Niño test grain markets in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 09/11/2026 Black Sea flows remain minimal The Black Sea picture is stark. Vessels sit at anchor offshore, waiting to enter the Danube to load, and the backlog is large. Ukrainian shipments from Izmail and Reni are vital for the export campaign, though volumes are relatively low. Only a few Russian shipments have been observed through the Black Sea during October, while Baltic Sea activity remains elevated. Fleet data shows a shift in vessel size rather than a fall in vessel numbers. The count of vessels in the Black Sea has not dropped, despite recent attacks on ships. Total deadweight is slipping slightly, because the Danube trade relies on smaller vessels. Romania and Bulgaria are the bright spots. Romanian exports are strong and Bulgarian outflows are stable. The TTS terminal in Romania ships domestic product and also transships Ukrainian grain that arrives by barge from the Danube. Ukraine faces a structural limit. The Danube river ports cannot export the same volume that its three major Black Sea ports can handle. Due to low prices and storage considerations, some farmers are reportedly delaying the corn harvest. Russia pivots to the Baltic, but capacity is the constraint Russian wheat is still being exported. The majority of cargoes now originate from Baltic ports such as Vysotsk, Ust-Luga, and St Petersburg. Wheat exports from these ports have been building, and have the potential to exceed records observed in September. Ust-Luga is a large industrial port zone where wheat competes for capacity with fertiliser and coal, both in strong demand. Rail wagons are piling up outside some ports, and domestic reports point to a shortage of wagons. Grain now travels about 2,000 kilometres north rather than a much shorter distance south, increasing the average voyage duration for Russian wheat. The numbers show progress, but a long way to go. September Baltic volumes reached a record of around 1 Mt, with potential for a stronger performance in October. Kpler estimates total Russian wheat exports close to 2.8 Mt for October, up from around 2.4 Mt in September. However, exports for either month remain close to half what has been seen in previous years. Overland exports are helping. Non-seaborne channels usually move 300,000 to 400,000 tonnes a month, but they have recently handled closer to 1 Mt. Importers split between paying up and waiting The loss of Russian and Ukrainian supply is reshaping import patterns. Wheat exports from July to September were the lowest start to a trade-year quarter since 2012. The Middle East and North Africa, which usually absorb the most Russian and Ukrainian grain, saw the largest drop. Behaviour varies by region. • Turkey is importing less Russian wheat, with only a small offset from Romanian supply. • Egypt, the world’s largest wheat importer, shows a seasonal lag. It had a good domestic crop but remains import dependent, and it is waiting for lower prices. • Indonesia is buying a larger volume of Argentine wheat earlier than usual, with harvest of Argentina’s crop supporting its export competitiveness. • The EU and Argentina are picking up displaced demand. Baltic EU grain is moving to Sub-Saharan Africa, and French wheat is winning more North African business. The US is close to import parity. The latest World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) cut 25 million bushels from the US export campaign, and a couple of Polish wheat shipments have reached the US. Price-sensitive buyers are rationing demand rather than switching origin, so Kpler estimates a slightly lower global wheat trade in 2026-27. Southern Hemisphere supply adds competition. Australia is near 30 Mt despite El Niño, and Argentina is at 21 to 22 Mt, relatively large compared to the past five to 10 years. In Russia, ex-farm prices are historically depressed, but alternatives to wheat are limited. Kpler analysts expect a small effect on planting, with spring weather mattering more for production. Freight firms as bunker costs bite Dry bulk earnings have risen through 2026. Panamax time charter earnings averaged near $18,500/day year-to-date, even after a recent dip. The Supramax equivalent has averaged just under $18,900/day over the same period. Panamaxes now carry around 60% of Australian coal, which competes with grain cargoes and lifts rates. Fuel is the other driver. Very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) at Singapore rose from $524 a tonne on 27 February to a peak of $1,140 on 10 March, in a sentiment-driven spike at the outbreak of the Middle East war. Prices have stayed well above pre-war levels. Kpler analysts expect tight fuel oil supply into 2027, because Gulf refineries remain down. On US Gulf to China freight via the Panama Canal, the bunker element rose from just over $6 a tonne before the war to above $13 at the peak. It is now close to $11 a tonne. A reroute via the Cape of Good Hope would add more. Vessel supply keeps a lid on owners. There are close to 260 Panamax ballasters in the Indian Ocean, against 170 a year ago and a five-year average of about 160. Many are heading to the Atlantic, probably in search of US cargo. Charterers may gain on hire rates, even as they pay more for fuel. Close to 150 ballasting Supramaxes are in the Black Sea and Mediterranean region, ahead of last year. This points to tighter logistics and congestion, partly from recent attacks on shipping and Danube barging problems. A return to normal trading would not be quick, with tester shipments first. Row crops: US corn burdened, soybeans tight China is expected to buy 25 Mt of US soybeans and has bought above 11 Mt so far. Our balance sheet assumes the full volume. That should let the US avoid competing on price elsewhere, yet current prices suggest it still does. Kpler estimates US soybean exports slightly above 50 Mt for 2026-27, with USDA lower, and ending stocks significantly below USDA. The May to July soybean spread is still in carry, and Kpler analysts highlight this could become inverted as stocks tighten. They remain bullish on the soybean to corn ratio. The ratio is at a high for the time of year, and fertiliser prices tilt next spring’s planting further towards soybeans. Corn is the opposite story. US sales lag last year, with Argentina and Brazil competing more strongly after two years of US dominance. Argentine corn sales are at a record, and sales for the coming year are the highest in five years. Kpler estimates US corn ending stocks slightly above 2 billion bushels, above the USDA’s latest forecast. Kpler’s estimate of 181 bu/ac for US yield, made before the latest WASDE, proved correct. In South America, Mato Grosso grows about 30% of Brazilian soybeans and is around 60% planted, ahead of its seasonal pace. Forecasts show little dryness so far, but El Niño could challenge yields over the next two months. Argentina usually receives good rainfall in El Niño years. Key watchpoints • Trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine are due to start from 10 November. Russia has so far opposed a maritime ceasefire, and the outcome is a wait and see. • Black Sea reopening. Our base case assumes no reopening. If it happens, Russian exports could reach 5 Mt in a month, Baltic and Black Sea combined. • Winter conditions and wagon availability in the Baltic, plus Egypt and other North African buyers returning to the market. • South American weather, especially rainfall in Mato Grosso, and the pace of US non-China soybean sales. Demand rationing is doing much of the work in wheat, but importers cannot wait forever. One more spike in prices looks likely, though it is unlikely to last. articles.title: IMO faces calls to enhance maritime security code amid rising threats
articles.summary: The International Association of Ports and Harbors has called on the International Maritime Organization to update the world’s main maritime security regulatory framework, as escalating attacks on commercial shipping and emerging cyber and technology risks expose potential gaps in rules largely unchanged for more...
articles.body: IMO faces calls to enhance maritime security code amid rising threats in International Shipping News 09/11/2026 The International Association of Ports and Harbors has called on the International Maritime Organization to update the world’s main maritime security regulatory framework, as escalating attacks on commercial shipping and emerging cyber and technology risks expose potential gaps in rules largely unchanged for more than two decades. In a statement Nov. 5, the industry group representing roughly 400 ports and related businesses globally said there was a case for updated guidance around the International Ship and Port Facility Security Code to reflect modern port operations and strengthen cooperation between governments and industry. Its survey of 181 maritime stakeholders rated the effectiveness of the existing framework at below 50% on average, with 83% identifying cybersecurity and digitalization as a weakness and 57% citing emerging technologies and automation. The debate comes amid severe disruption to key energy shipping routes amid persistent security concerns. The International Maritime Organization has recorded over 120 incidents around the Strait of Hormuz, possibly more than 100 attacks in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, and 19 attacks or piracy incidents in the Gulf of Aden and Western Indian Ocean region this year, resulting in 24 verified seafarer deaths and potentially another 38 casualties. Despite a recovery in recent months, S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data shows Middle Eastern crude and refined products exports in October averaged 18.8 million barrels per day — just 72% of the level seen before the outbreak of US-Iran war in late February. Jeremy Greenwood, head of the IMO’s Maritime Security Section, welcomed further discussion on the ISPS code but stressed that increasing threats did not necessarily mean the regulation itself was fundamentally flawed. “I would argue that we may have more of an implementation problem than we have an instrument problem,” Greenwood told the IAPH World Ports Conference in London Nov. 5. Adopted in 2002 and mandatory since 2004 under the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, the ISPS Code sets security requirements for ships and ports, covering access controls, threat assessments, security plans and operational procedures. Code revamp A US proposal this year said the code had not undergone a significant revision since adoption despite evolving security threats to merchant shipping. Timothy Brown, chief of the Office of Standards Evaluation and Development at the US Coast Guard, said cyberattacks and anti-drone measures involved “very different threat factors that just did not exist 20 years ago.” Security disruption also has direct consequences for commodity markets, with attacks or tighter security measures potentially disrupting cargo operations, constraining vessel availability and raising freight and insurance costs. “Anything that creates that friction in the port reduces the efficiency of the port, reduces the efficiency of the supply chain and has both security and economic implications,” Brown said in the conference. Peter Van Parys, COO of North Sea Port and chair of IAPH’s Risk & Resilience Committee, called for a more effective framework rather than simply expanding regulation, saying the industry needed “not a bigger ISPS, but perhaps a more effective one” that focuses on emerging risks and scrutinize outcome of implementation. The IMO is due to hold the next meeting of the Maritime Safety Committee during Dec. 14-18, where proposals concerning the ISPS framework and wider port security are tabled for discussion. articles.body: Before a Port Call: Inside Alpha Bulkers Shipmanagement Inc.’s Approach to PSC Readiness in International Shipping News 09/11/2026 Preparing for a Port State Control (PSC) inspection means understanding how a vessel’s condition, history and trading pattern intersect with the inspection priorities of its next port. Exposure varies between ports and PSC regimes, making it important for ship and shore teams to understand where closer attention may be needed. That preparation also depends on work carried out long before arrival: maintaining equipment, developing crew knowledge and applying lessons from previous inspections. By analysing data and turning them into reliable, contextual and actionable insight, risk intelligence can help teams focus their attention, with company procedures and professional judgement guiding how they act on it. For Alpha Bulkers Shipmanagement Inc., bringing these elements together is central to improving PSC performance across its active fleet of 33 dry bulk vessels. The company combines crew assessment, technical preparation and fleet-wide learning with RightShip’s PSC RiskIQ to help identify potential exposure earlier and prepare accordingly. The company is seeing measurable progress. Its PSC Deficiency Performance Index—the average number of deficiencies recorded per PSC inspection across the fleet—improved from approximately 2.40 in 2025 to 1.4 as of September 2026. It had also recorded no PSC detentions as of September 2026, compared with four in 2025. The focus now is on sustaining that progress and working towards a more demanding internal target through a disciplined approach involving people, procedures and intelligence. Readiness Starts Before Joining The Vessel The company set out to improve consistency in how vessels across its fleet prepare for PSC inspections. Different ports and inspection regimes bring different risk profiles, while developing practical knowledge, familiarity with company procedures and onboard safety culture takes sustained effort. “We treat PSC performance as a continuous ship-and-shore process rather than something that starts shortly before an inspection”, says Capt. Andreas Togantzis, HSQE & Marine Manager at Alpha Bulkers Shipmanagement Inc. One part of that process is a rank-specific pre-joining assessment being implemented for all officers and crew. It assesses their familiarity with the company’s Safety Management System (SMS), procedures and responsibilities relevant to their rank, helping establish a stronger understanding of expectations before they step aboard. Once onboard, vessel teams follow company PSC procedures and checklists, supported by shore personnel who review inspection trends, recurring deficiencies and individual vessel exposure. Inspection findings inform reviews of planned maintenance instructions and SMS procedures, while lessons are shared transparently across the fleet. This creates a continuing connection between inspection experience, company guidance and the preparation of crews and vessels. Understanding The Exposure Ahead Within this wider approach, Alpha Bulkers Shipmanagement Inc uses PSC RiskIQ to make preparation more focused on the vessel and its upcoming ports. The team uses PSC RiskIQ information on a port-by-port and vessel-by-vessel basis, alongside its own SMS procedures, planned maintenance requirements and PSC checklists. “PSC RiskIQ helps us better understand that exposure in advance and allows both vessel and shore teams to focus preparation more effectively” Capt. Andreas Togantzis explains Information from the tool and relevant checklists is disseminated throughout the fleet, so Masters, Chief Engineers and shore personnel can work from the same understanding of potential exposure. That shared view helps teams direct attention towards areas that may warrant closer preparation. The approach is particularly relevant in trading areas such as Australia and China, where the company reports significant PSC exposure. Australia represents a substantial part of the fleet’s trading pattern. For China calls, the company has also introduced third-party pre-PSC inspections during discharge operations as an additional preventive measure. PSC RiskIQ provides another layer of intelligence within this preparation framework. Vessel and shore teams bring that information together with company requirements and their operational knowledge to guide their work. Progress Across A Broader Programme In his September 2026 update, Andreas reported that Alpha Bulkers Shipmanagement Inc.’s PSC Deficiency Performance Index had improved from approximately 2.40 in 2025 to 1.4 in 2026 to date. The company had also recorded zero PSC detentions in 2026 to date, compared with four during the full year of 2025. The company sees these as encouraging indications that its approach is moving performance in the right direction. The improvement reflects a coordinated programme across the company rather than any single initiative. That programme brings together stronger vessel preparation, continuous review of maintenance and SMS requirements, fleet-wide learning and greater ship-and-shore involvement. Pre-joining assessments, targeted third-party inspections and quarterly management reviews also form part of the effort. Within this wider approach, PSC RiskIQ plays a clear role in helping teams understand potential exposure and prepare more effectively. “For us, PSC RiskIQ has been assisting our Seafarers and Office Staff to understand potential exposure earlier and make preparation more focused and risk-based” – says Capt. Andreas Togantzis The value of the intelligence lies in how teams incorporate it into this work: understanding potential exposure earlier, focusing preparation and maintaining a shared risk picture between vessel and office. Learning From Every Inspection Alpha Bulkers’ internal objective remains a fleet average below 1.0 deficiency per PSC inspection. Performance is improving, but the company recognises that it has further to go. Its priorities are to continue developing crew competence, strengthening technical readiness and using inspection experience to improve company procedures. PSC RiskIQ will remain part of that process, supporting assessment of potential exposure before vessels arrive at their next port. “Our objective is not simply to achieve a temporary improvement in statistics, but to build a more consistent level of readiness, knowledge and awareness across the fleet. PSC RiskIQ is one of the tools that can support us in achieving that objective” – says Capt. Andreas Togantzis For Alpha Bulkers Shipmanagement Inc., each inspection provides knowledge that can strengthen preparation for the next port call. By bringing that learning together with earlier visibility of potential exposure, the company is building on its progress while continuing to raise the level of readiness across its fleet. Use vessel- and port-specific risk intelligence to focus preparation, prioritise attention and support more informed decisions across ship and shore. Approximately 10,000 vessels now have access to PSC RiskIQ to help prepare for and manage port calls. Over a one-year period, customers actively using PSC RiskIQ recorded 18% fewer deficiencies and 12% fewer detentions compared with industry. articles.body: Maersk Asia Pacific Market Update – November 2026 in International Shipping News 09/11/2026 Gemini Network Enhancements Bring New Asia–Europe Connectivity Options Maersk has announced further enhancements to the Gemini network1, with changes to port coverage and routing options between Asia and Europe scheduled for implementation throughout November. The adjustments will strengthen connectivity across key European and Mediterranean gateways, while introducing additional options for shipments connecting to destinations in West Africa and Latin America. The enhancements reflect ongoing efforts to improve network connectivity and provide customers with greater routing flexibility across international trade corridors. As changes are introduced across individual services, available departure options, transit times and port connections may vary depending on the origin and destination. For customers, the developments provide an opportunity to review existing shipping arrangements and assess whether new connections could better support their supply-chain requirements. Checking updated sailing schedules and coordinating shipment plans with logistics partners can help businesses align cargo movements with production schedules, inventory needs and delivery commitments. East Asia Port Recovery Update Operational conditions at major East China ports have improved following earlier seasonal weather disruptions, and vessel waiting times continue to decline compared with previous weeks. While the direct effects of these disruptions have largely eased, the regional port network is closely connected, so conditions at one location can still affect cargo flows and schedules elsewhere. Strong export activity from Asia continues to put pressure on some congested ports, and certain key regional hubs remain under pressure. As a result, sailing schedules across the wider network are still adjusting as operations progressively normalise. Recent industry data points in the same direction: port conditions are easing, although schedule performance has yet to fully recover. According to Drewry’s November Container Shipping Market Signals, average port waiting times declined by 16% month on month to 1.4 days in October.2 However, schedule reliability remains an area to monitor, with Sea-Intelligence reporting continued variations in vessel arrivals across major East–West trades.3 For customers, these developments highlight the value of maintaining visibility over shipment schedules as regional operations stabilise. Reviewing confirmed departure and arrival dates, allowing flexibility around cargo cut-offs and coordinating onward transport arrangements can help businesses manage delivery requirements through November. Year-End Ocean Planning Calls for Close Attention to Sailing Schedules As businesses prepare for year-end inventory requirements and upcoming delivery commitments, ocean shipping conditions continue to evolve across major trade lanes. Seasonal changes in cargo requirement, alongside adjustments to vessel services and sailing schedules, are influencing available shipping options as November progresses. Recent analysis from Drewry and Sea-Intelligence points to schedule reliability remaining under pressure.2 3 Together, these trends suggest that sailing availability and transit times may still vary between individual services, origins and destinations. For customers, early coordination between production, shipping and distribution teams can help maintain flexibility through the year-end period. Reviewing available departures, cargo cut-off requirements and onward transport arrangements, while sharing shipment forecasts with logistics partners, can help businesses align cargo movements with inventory needs and delivery commitments through November and December. Air Freight Market Update Air Freight Peak Season: Key Dates and Planning Considerations Air freight activity across Asia Pacific continues to be supported by technology-related shipments, including semiconductors, AI infrastructure components and high-value electronics. Recent data from the International Air Transport Association (IATA) shows that Asia Pacific airlines recorded an 8.6% year-on-year increase in air cargo activity in September.4 As the year-end peak season progresses, major retail events, holiday periods and preparations for Chinese New Year/Lunar New Year are bringing additional considerations for air freight planning. The calendar below highlights key dates and practical steps customers can take to manage shipment requirements through the coming months. Mekong Dry Season Brings Planning Considerations for Inland Cargo Mekong barge operations are currently unaffected, with water levels remaining within normal operating ranges. However, forecasts suggest that drier conditions during the 2026–27 dry season could lead to lower river levels between December and April, which may affect vessel loading practices and schedule planning on some inland waterways. The areas most likely to be monitored include Mekong Delta waterways and the Vietnam–Phnom Penh cross-border barge corridor, which support cargo movements within the Mekong region. While it is too early to determine whether any operational impact will occur, customers moving agricultural, food and temperature-controlled cargo may wish to stay informed of local developments as the dry season progresses. At present, no disruption is expected. However, customers may benefit from maintaining visibility of shipment plans, allowing reasonable flexibility in transit schedules and discussing alternative transport arrangements with logistics partners where appropriate. Reefer shippers may also wish to review cargo handover and storage arrangements in advance of peak harvesting and shipping periods. For customers using Mekong inland waterways, monitoring conditions through the dry season and maintaining flexibility in transport planning can help support smooth cargo flows should operating conditions change. Inland Transport Conditions as Year-End Approaches As businesses move towards the end of the year, inland logistics activity across Asia Pacific continues to be shaped by seasonal activity and changing shipment requirements. In China, recent figures from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing indicate continued expansion in logistics activity, with September’s Logistics Performance Index remaining in growth territory for the fifth consecutive month. The federation has also highlighted expectations of stronger road freight activity during the fourth quarter, supported by industrial activity and year-end e-commerce movements. While the impact of the Double 11 shopping festival on first-mile container movements is expected to be limited, the approaching year-end shipping period may bring changes in trucking requirements and equipment availability on selected routes. Similar year-end pressures are emerging across Southeast Asia, where inland operations are also facing growing pressure around key port and industrial areas. Reports of depot congestion in some Southeast markets highlight potential challenges for container movements, and rising year-end volumes are likely to add pressure on trucking availability and turnaround times. In Malaysia and Singapore, developments in transport and operational conditions are also being monitored as the year-end period approaches. For customers, these developments reinforce the importance of coordinating inland transport with production and ocean shipping schedules. Providing early visibility of expected volumes, securing trucking requirements where possible and planning empty container pick-up and return arrangements carefully can help businesses manage potential constraints. Allowing flexibility around collection and delivery schedules, particularly in areas experiencing depot congestion, can also support smoother cargo movements through the year-end period. Early Chinese New Year Brings Forward Supply Chain Planning With Chinese New Year falling on 6 February 2027, businesses sourcing and shipping goods from China face a shorter planning window than in 2026, when the holiday began on 17 February. The earlier date may bring forward production deadlines, cargo collection requirements and inland transport arrangements as manufacturers prepare for the holiday period. Recent industry guidance from SEKO Logistics highlights the importance of starting preparations early, noting that factory closures and the subsequent return to normal production can extend beyond the official holiday period. As businesses seek to complete shipments ahead of these closures, requirements for inland transport, container equipment and terminal delivery slots may become more concentrated on certain routes. For customers, providing early visibility of expected shipment volumes and inland transport requirements will be particularly important, especially for trucking and other time-sensitive movements. Confirming supplier production schedules, cargo-ready dates and container equipment needs in advance can help logistics partners plan resources and reduce exposure to short-notice constraints. Allowing for a gradual return to production following the holiday can also support inventory and distribution planning into the first quarter of 2027. Trade Environment Update EU Carbon Requirements Affect Selected Asia Pacific Exports The EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which entered its definitive phase in January 2026, introduces additional compliance requirements for selected carbon-intensive imports, including iron, steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers and hydrogen. While the measure applies to a relatively narrow range of products, exporters of affected goods from Asia Pacific may need to provide production and emissions data to support their EU customers’ reporting obligations. For businesses handling these products, recent European Commission guidance5 reinforces the importance of reviewing product classifications, emissions data and documentation processes. Early coordination with EU importers and compliance teams can help businesses prepare for reporting requirements and assess potential cost implications. articles.summary: Xeneta, the AI-powered ocean and air freight intelligence solution, today announced its largest set of product launches at the 10th annual Xeneta Summit, Munich. articles.body: Xeneta announces new AI-native capabilities with a tender product and an MCP connector, new Air and the industry’s first view of transshipment in International Shipping News 09/11/2026 Xeneta, the AI-powered ocean and air freight intelligence solution, today announced its largest set of product launches at the 10th annual Xeneta Summit, Munich. Presented live to over 600 shippers, forwarders and carriers, the launches mark a shift in what Xeneta does for its customers. For 14 years, Xeneta has given freight procurement the data to see the market; now it moves into the decisions that data informs and the actions that follow. The launches span three areas: new data, led by the first dataset to show both the announced and the actual transit time of cargo moving via a transshipment hub and an air benchmark covering over 17M tonnes of airfreight on 92% more lanes than before; AI Agents with embedded Xeneta freight expertise reading a customer’s contracts against the market and recommending what to do first; and new execution tools, Xeneta Rate Management (XRM) and Xeneta Tender, that put the live market rate next to every contract and every bid, so teams manage rates and award tenders on evidence they can defend. Fabio Brocca, Xeneta Chief Product Officer, told the Summit: “Procurement teams are hired to decide, but they spend their days buried in data. For 14 years Xeneta has given them the most trusted benchmark in the industry. This year we put that benchmark inside the work itself, so you can see what is happening, decide with confidence and act, all in one place.” See: the data foundation grows Every launch stands on the same foundation: more than 850 million contracted rates across 170,000 ocean port pairs, updated daily, sourced from shipper and forwarder contracts rather than carriers; air rates, volumes and load factors across around 18,000 airport pairs, refreshed weekly; and schedule and reliability data on more than 7,500 vessels across 50,000 port pairs, showing the promised voyage against the actual one. Transshipment, the transit time nobody could see A large share of containerized cargo moves on transshipment routes, and until now shippers planned on the transit time the carrier promised and found out the truth too late. The new Xeneta Transshipment dataset shows how long shipments really take on indirect routes, by carrier and by hub, promised against actual, taking Xeneta total ocean coverage to 27,000 lanes. Built on the AIS vessel movement data behind Ocean Schedules and data models developed by Xeneta, it shows what the ships actually did, side by side with what the timetable said. With it, procurement and planning teams can pick the carriers and hubs that arrive on time on their lanes, cut the safety stock they hold against late arrivals and stop paying for transit time they never get. Brocca said: “So far the industry has benchmarked the price of a container. Nobody could benchmark the time, because part of the journey was hidden. Transshipment makes that part visible.” Transshipment is available now as an add-on for existing Xeneta Ocean customers. It complements Ocean Schedules, live since March, which tracks more than 7,500 vessels across 50,000 port pairs and places the carrier’s published schedule next to the actual voyage. New Xeneta Air, rebuilt to cover 45,000 airport pairs Xeneta Air now covers approximately 18,000 lanes and is the only air freight benchmark built from both sides of the market: what shippers pay and what airlines fly. Shipper rates sit next to airline rates, volumes and load factors across 13 parameters that help buyers make better procurement decisions, including five special cargo types: pharma, perishables, live animals, valuables and dangerous goods. Air Datalink delivers lanes and time series straight into the customer’s BI tool. Brocca said: “Air has been priced on month-old averages for too long. With both sides of the market in one view, refreshed every week, air freight buyers finally get the same clarity ocean buyers have had for a decade.” Decide: AI that recommends, wherever you work AI Agents in the platform, now generally available Two agents answer the two questions every procurement team asks. The Portfolio Spend Optimization agent answers “where am I overpaying?”: it spots every lane above market, ranks them by savings and flags them before the contract renews. The Supplier Spend Optimization agent answers “which suppliers should I challenge?”: it shows how each carrier and forwarder performs against the market and suggests who to challenge and who to lock in. B rocca said: “What we’ve built means that in a few clicks, Xeneta shows you where the money is going and what you can do about it. The agent gives you a recommendation, but the decision stays with you, and now you’re making it with the numbers already in front of you.” Ask Xeneta, the MCP connector for AI assistants Not every rate decision is made inside Xeneta. Ask Xeneta is a Model Context Protocol (MCP) connector that puts Xeneta data and agents inside the AI assistants customers already use. Users can ask it to benchmark rates on a lane, by market or by carrier, check a contract against the market, and the answer comes from Xeneta data. Ask Xeneta is in exclusive early access, and sign-up opened at the Summit. Brocca said: “We didn’t want to build yet another tool that people have to log into. Ask Xeneta brings our data and our agents into the AI assistants our customers are already working in, so the market view is right there when they’re actually making the decision.” Custom AI Agents For teams that want AI to do the work, not only recommend it, Xeneta now builds Custom AI Agents directly into the customer’s IT environment with connections to their existing systems, deployed by Xeneta engineers in weeks. The agents run spot bids, quotes, rate updates and reports, and check every step against the live market rate. This service is available now and sold separately. Brocca said: “Other AI agents can fill in a tender or process a quote. Only ours knows what the market rate is, so it can tell you when a quote is too high.” Act: workflows that do the work for you Most procurement teams still run their rates and tenders in tools never designed for freight: spreadsheets, generic sourcing suites and email threads, with multiple versions, slow amendments and every team on a different file. XRM and Xeneta Tender replace that with workflows where every rate and every bid sits next to the market. Xeneta Rate Management: AI ingestion, Rate Adjustments and a first step into allocations XRM, launched at last year’s Summit, now holds customers’ full rate books, including inland, surcharges and other variables beyond the ocean rate, benchmarked against the market daily. Customers can now hand XRM any rate sheet and let the AI map it: it reads the columns, standardizes the values and asks only when unsure. When a carrier changes a surcharge mid-contract, they apply the change from whatever arrived, an incomplete Excel, a PDF, a Word file or an email, and XRM updates every rate it touches in one confirmed step. A quarterly BAF change no longer means re-uploading the whole contract. The Rate Adjustments pilot, starting this quarter, goes one step further: customers copy Xeneta on carrier rate-change emails and the update lands in XRM ready to review, so no surcharge is ever retyped or lost. It is the first step towards a rate book that keeps itself up to date. XRM Allocations, with a first release by the end of 2026, lets shippers import booking data and see actual volume against the minimum committed to each carrier, per rate and per contract. Brocca said: “XRM gives you every rate from every supplier in one place in minutes, not weeks, and keeps the record current and error-free, so Finance and Procurement get a number they can trust. Gone are the days of hunting through email threads for the surcharge somebody agreed months before.” Xeneta Tender preview The benchmark a procurement team uses all year is the one thing it has no time for during a tender. Xeneta Tender changes that without changing how a team works. Users bring their tender files, rules and templates as they are, in any format, and drag and drop. Tender then show every bid next to the market rate and the metrics that matter beside it, so an overpriced bid stands out instantly and the award is made with the full picture in view. Tender can also simulate any scenario a buyer describes in plain language and show the acctual spend with clarity. Tender is in exclusive early access to selected customers with general availability planned for 2027. Brocca said: “Tender is where everything comes together. The data you trust, the agents that spot the outliers and the workflow that gets you to an award you can defend in front of your CFO.” From benchmark to workflow The launches are the next chapter in Xeneta’s plan to build one integrated decision platform for freight procurement: neutral market data, service performance, AI that recommends, and the workflows where rates are managed and tenders are run. articles.summary: An electric shock can cause burns, serious injuries, even death. articles.body: Electric shock: a hidden danger in everyday shipboard work in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 09/11/2026 An electric shock can cause burns, serious injuries, even death. The outcome depends on factors including the voltage, the amount of current, as well as the path and time that the current takes to pass through the body. It does not take a large current through the body to cause serious harm. The US Occupational Safety and Health Administration notes that currents above 10 milliamperes can cause involuntary muscle contractions. At higher levels, consequences can include extreme pain, respiratory arrest and possible death. The rhythmic pumping of the heart ceases at around 1 amp. Voltage also matters because it helps drive current through resistance. Electrical systems on ships operate at different voltages, from low-voltage signal equipment to switchboards operating above 1,000 volts. Generally speaking, care should be exercised when the voltage exceeds 50 volts. The actual danger depends on the circumstances, including the condition of equipment, the electrical system and the environment in which work is carried out. Water, sweat and humidity all increase conductivity on the body’s surface, thus increases the risk on ships. The risk points onboard Ships have several electrical distribution systems and voltages vary from as low as 5 volts for signal power to well over 1000 volts in switchboards. This is typically stepped down to 440 volts for machinery and 220 volts for lighting and sockets used for portable equipment. The Liberia Maritime Authority (LMA) recently published a Marine Advisory on the prevention of electrocution casualties with particular emphasis on portable electrical equipment. A review of Gard cases draws many parallels with the LMA Advisory, as outlined in the below examples. Lighting Portable lights were the main feature of the LMA’s case studies with portable lights connected to the shipboard power supply. In one Gard case a crew member died using a portable lamp for cargo operations. The investigation found that the light was incorrectly wired, resulting in the light housing being energized. Further insights into similar accidents can be found in this flag state report, one of which identified a joint in the lamp’s electrical cable that had been wrapped in electrical tape and in another the use of a “homemade” cable. There is a very high risk of electrocution upon touching an improperly wired metal object, with the human body becoming the path of least resistance for electricity to reach the ground. In another Gard case, a senior crew member died repairing fixed lighting in the accommodation without first isolating the electrical supply. The UK’s Code of Safe Working Practices (COSWP) references the Lock Out Tag Out (LOTO) safety procedure that ensures power sources are properly isolated, shut off and cannot be started up again before work on live systems is completed. RightShip’s Safety Insight refers to an underutilization of this safety protocol based on inspections. Grinding Portable angle electric grinders are another well used tool on board for rust removal, weld preparation, and cutting metal. In one Gard case, a crew member died due to electrocution using a grinder for routine maintenance. The investigation pointed to an electrical fault with the tool. A flag state investigation into another accident with a grinder references an electric shock before the crew member suffered a fatal cut from the grinder. The investigators considered the possibility of electric shock causing muscle spasm. As mentioned above, muscle contractions can mean the person cannot ‘let go’ and the shock can cause involuntary reactions. Welding Welding is another common activity onboard, which had fatal consequences for one crew member in a Gard case. The work task was to repair a pipe leak in the engine room. After the work was completed, a member of the work team was discovered alone and unconscious with burn injuries. The welding machine had not been switched off, and the deceased crew was found on the steel deck, missing some personal protective equipment (PPE). A flag state investigation into another fatal accident involved a welding repair to railings on the main deck. Although proper PPE was worn, intermittent rain showers before and during the hot work were considered the probable cause of the electrocution. The welding machine was an older type using AC power with an idling voltage of more than three times the recommended level. UK COSWP was referenced in the vessel’s SMS and recommends welding machines with a DC rather than AC output. If DC cannot be used, UK COSWP requires a voltage-limiting device. The investigation also identified an unsafe cable set-up. The return cable, which should have been clamped directly to the workpiece to limit the area carrying current, was instead connected to the welding machine’s storage rack in the forecastle. This significantly increased the area exposed to electric current. The danger to first responders In some accidents, first responders have also suffered an electric shock. Much like enclosed space rescues, responder safety must take precedence over instinct. Electrical power sources should be isolated before tending to the injured person. For further guidance on responding to someone suffering an electric shock, see the Mariners Medico Guide. Performance Influence Factors (PIFs) PIFs are human factors that may enhance or diminish performance. Applying industry recognised PIFs to the above referenced electrocution cases, offers the following insights: • Recognising safety criticality. Electrical hazards can be underestimated during routine work. This reflects the finding in Gard’s 2026 Crew Claims report that most injuries happen during planned, everyday operations. Risk assessments should consider electrical hazards, particularly when using equipment in wet, damp or humid conditions. There should be no assumption that portable tools will always be safe to use, especially those subject to wear, tear, and rough handling. LMA’s Advisory also pinpointed the risks associated with manually relocating portable lamps whilst still energized, pointing to a need to reinforce crew training and risk awareness. • Follow safe procedures. Power should be isolated before working on electrical equipment, and appropriate PPE used when required. Experience alone does not prevent accidents. Inspections and audits should therefore check whether actual working practices match written procedures. • Clear and understandable procedures. In some cases, SMS procedures were limited to managing risks with higher voltage fixed equipment and were otherwise vague in relation to portable equipment. Procedures for portable equipment should include appropriate inspection, testing and maintenance by competent personnel. Maintaining a register of portable electrical equipment can support this. • Team dynamics and communications. In several cases the crew members were alone when they were electrocuted, bringing into question the adequacy of supervision or, where necessary, the requirements of a Permit to Work. Working alone can result in delayed discovery and first aid. Good communication is especially important when electrical isolation is remote from the worksite. Crew should also feel empowered to question unsafe conditions and to exercise stop work authority. • Stress, workload, fatigue. These factors are often overlooked in accident investigations, and fatigue was positively ruled out in only one reported case. In another, documented hours of rest complied with STCW/MLC requirements; however, records may not always reflect actual conditions experienced by crew. Some of the accidents occurred in the morning when Gard’s Crew Claims Report found the highest concentration of injuries. Operational pressures, adjustment, and fatigue may all play an important role in accident risk during morning hours. • Motivation to get the job done. These are also factors that can be overlooked in investigations and may affect decision making skills. In one case, a senior rank left the afternoon break to re-start work alone, perhaps motivated to get the job done sooner rather than later. • Workplace ergonomics, including signage, tools, layout, space, noise, light, heat, etc. The UK COSWP recommends low-voltage (max 50 volt) supplies for portable tools and lamps, especially for work locations that are damp, humid or have large conductive surfaces. When it is not practical to use low voltages, UK COSWP references alternative precautions. These include Residual Current Device (RCD) protection, which monitors and detects electricity flowing down an unintended path and quickly switches off the electricity. • Human-Machine Interface (Controls, Alarms, etc.). Electrical equipment differs from ship to ship and electrical standards vary across countries. This can be particularly relevant for portable equipment and crew must understand how individual safety features work and are maintained. • Opportunity to learn and practice. The gap between basic theoretical training and real-world task execution can be critical given the unseen risk of electrocution. A Walk Through or Talk Through process together with a competent colleague can make all the difference. Fostering a psychologically safe culture of trust where employees can ask questions and report mistakes is also important for continuous organizational learning. Conclusion Accidents featured in this article speak to the unseen – and sometimes fatal – risk to crew from electrocution. The risk arises during planned, everyday operations, and with commonly used tools or electrical systems with well-known dangers. Crew performance during these operations is usually influenced by wider factors and is rarely rooted in a sole mistake. Companies are encouraged to seek out and understand these factors, especially from accidents or near misses with less severe outcomes but high severity potential. The insights will help to manage risks in future operations through safety leaders onboard. Ultimately however, everyone has a role in safe work. All individuals involved in a task should take time to consider whether it involves electrocution risk, as well as the factors putting themselves and others more at risk. A final pause to imagine the consequences of not taking the right steps can be a lifesaver. articles.body: MMI Daily Iron Ore Index Report November 9 2026 in Chinese iron ore and steelmaking prices 09/11/2026 Iron ore prices combined stability with weakness today. DCE most-traded closed unchanged at 687.5 yuan/mt, and all eight major Qingdao port product quotations were steady. The 61% and 65% port indices each fell 1 yuan while the 58% rose 1 yuan. Seaborne 61% and 65% indices declined to USD 91.50 and 107.60/dmt, and all 12 brands eased against the previous report. Different moves in composite indices and product quotations highlight resource composition and pricing bases; no single market alone establishes broad strengthening or weakening. Incoming supply and physical consumption remain central. Chinese arrivals rose 33.30% WoW in the week to Nov 6, while global shipments fell 7.89%; voyage lags and reporting periods can produce divergence. Latest ten-port stocks rose 643,600 mt from the previous period, while surveyed daily hot metal fell 4,800 mt. Higher arrivals may increase subsequent absorption pressure, but do not establish that current inventories have already risen further. A cautious, range-bound near-term view remains appropriate. Steady futures and major port quotations, together with relative low-grade resilience, offer some support. Lower seaborne prices, existing stock accumulation and slightly weaker hot metal limit upside momentum. Better mill orders and margins accompanied by sustained purchasing could strengthen support; difficulty absorbing arrivals and predominantly needs-based restocking could leave ore prices fluctuating under pressure. articles.body: Americas Europe Offshore DOF wins more AHTS work offshore Canada Bojan Lepic November 9, 2026 0 340 1 minute read MarineTraffic / Leo Lohofener MarineTraffic / Leo Lohofener Norwegian offshore vessel owner DOF has secured a contract extension for its anchor handling tug supply (AHTS) vessel Skandi Mariner , which is working offshore Canada. The company said an option under the vessel’s existing charter had been exercised, extending its firm employment from the second quarter of 2027 until the third quarter of 2028. The extension is valued between $15m and $25m While DOF did not identify the customer in its latest announcement, its earlier investor presentations state that the vessel has been working for Canadian energy company Cenovus Energy. The 2017-built Skandi Mariner secured an initial two-year contract with Cenovus, commencing in the second quarter of 2025, to support the development of the White Rose field offshore Newfoundland. The 95-metre vessel entered the Canadian market alongside the Skandi Mover , which secured a separate 5.5-year agreement with the same operator. Both vessels were involved in the tow-out of the West White Rose concrete gravity structure during 2025. The latest extension gives Skandi Mariner more than a year of additional firm employment in the Canadian offshore market, where DOF has built a substantial fleet presence following its acquisition of Maersk Supply Service’s offshore business in late 2024.
