articles.body: Exploration & Production November 9, 2026 · 1 minute ago Thanks to good results, Vaalco proceeds to second exploration phase at block off Côte d'Ivoire NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Vaalco's operations in Côte D'Ivoire. Source: Vaalco Energy Houston-based Vaalco Energy has completed the first exploration phase at its block offshore Côte d'Ivoire and is now proceeding to the second following good results. Vaalco farmed into and became the operator of exploration license CI-705 located offshore Côte d'Ivoire in March 2025, holding a 70% working interest. The U.S. company reported today, November 9, that it had completed the first exploration phase work commitments, which included the evaluation and interpretation of existing seismic and well data. Thanks to the results from this first phase, Vaalco decided to progress to the second exploration phase, with government approval secured. This phase includes further seismic reprocessing, relinquishing 25% of the exploration block and a commitment to drill an exploration well by the end of 2028. The CI-705 block is located in the prolific Ivoirien Basin and is approximately 70 kilometers to the west of Vaalco’s CI-40 Block, where the Baobab and Kossipo oil fields are located; “We are pleased with the results of the First Exploration Phase and are excited to move into the Second Exploration Phase. We see encouraging prospectivity on the block in the play types proven throughout the Ivoirien Basin including both structural and stratigraphic traps in the Upper Cretaceous and Albian sections," said George Maxwell , Vaalco’s Chief Executive Officer. "Recent nearby discoveries are on trend with CI-705 and, provide additional validation of our play concepts and our view of the block’s prospectivity. Our continued success and organic project pipeline support Vaalco’s strategic focus on growing production, reserves and value for our shareholders.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.body: Containers Europe Greater China Shipyards A2B-online turns to China for methanol-ready boxship pair Adis Ajdin November 9, 2026 0 317 1 minute read A2B-online A2B-online Dutch shortsea container operator A2B-online has ordered two more methanol-capable vessels at China Merchants Industry Weihai Shipyard, doubling its fleet renewal programme to four ships. The latest contract marks a switch to China after the company booked its first two newbuildings at Turkey’s Sedef Shipyard in 2023. The Chinese pair will feature multi-fuel methanol propulsion, shore power connections and battery systems, allowing emission-free operations in ports and inland waterways. A2B-online said the newbuildings will follow the same design approach developed with Hamburg-based engineering firm Technolog Services, offering double the cargo intake of its older tonnage without a significant increase in vessel length. No contract price, delivery dates or capacity figures have been disclosed for the latest two ships. The vessels will eventually be deployed on the company’s shortsea network linking Moerdijk in the Netherlands with Tilbury, Immingham and Teesport in the UK. The latest investment follows the carrier’s 2023 order for two 650 teu methanol-capable containerships at Sedef. Those vessels, A2B Vision and A2B Progress, have been launched and are preparing to enter service. A2B-online’s existing fleet comprises seven older Sietas-built containerships dating from 1995 to 1999, which the company is progressively replacing with more efficient tonnage. The latest orders will extend that replacement programme to four vessels, with the new ships designed to carry significantly more cargo while maintaining dimensions suited to the operator’s established North Sea services. articles.summary: Offshore drilling contractor Ocean Oilfield has secured a contract from Tende Energy to deploy its Ocean MVM jackup rig for a drilling campaign offshore Tunisia. The rig will be used for the Abiod well programme on the Maâmoura concession in the Gulf of Hammamet, targeting a previously undeveloped fractured carbonate...
articles.body: Africa Middle East Offshore Tende Energy hires rig for drilling work offshore Tunisia Bojan Lepic November 9, 2026 0 450 1 minute read Noble Corp Noble Corp Offshore drilling contractor Ocean Oilfield has secured a contract from Tende Energy to deploy its Ocean MVM jackup rig for a drilling campaign offshore Tunisia. The rig will be used for the Abiod well programme on the Maâmoura concession in the Gulf of Hammamet, targeting a previously undeveloped fractured carbonate reservoir. The Ocean MVM jackup was previously named Noble Resolve and was sold by Noble Corporation to Ocean Oilfield for $64m in cash in December 2025. The planned work involves drilling a deviated sidetrack from the existing Maâmoura E2 well to bring additional hydrocarbons into production through infrastructure already in place. According to technical information published by Anglo Tunisian Oil & Gas, the proposed Abiod well could deliver gross production exceeding 6,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, subject to successful drilling and reservoir performance. The reservoir was discovered in 1987 and subsequently appraised in 1988, when testing demonstrated oil and gas flows. The development concept envisages routing production to the existing Tazarka processing facilities, avoiding the need for an entirely new offshore production platform. The Maâmoura field is located in approximately 58 m of water and forms part of Tende’s wider Tunisian offshore portfolio, which also includes the neighbouring Baraka concession. Tende holds a 49% operated interest in Maâmoura, with Tunisia’s state-owned ETAP controlling the remaining 51%. The ownership structure changed earlier this year after Eni’s Tunisia subsidiary transferred its previous interest to Tende. articles.title: Boluda buys Dutch offshore towage specialist
articles.summary: Spanish towage giant Boluda has acquired Dutch offshore towage and heavy transport specialist Muller Dordrecht, adding 16 tugs and eight barges to its growing global fleet. The takeover gives Boluda full ownership of the century-old family business, whose fleet includes seven offshore tugs specialising in complex...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables Boluda buys Dutch offshore towage specialist Bojan Lepic November 9, 2026 0 263 1 minute read Muller Dordrecht Muller Dordrecht Spanish towage giant Boluda has acquired Dutch offshore towage and heavy transport specialist Muller Dordrecht, adding 16 tugs and eight barges to its growing global fleet. The takeover gives Boluda full ownership of the century-old family business, whose fleet includes seven offshore tugs specialising in complex marine transportation, rig moves, anchor handling and offshore wind projects. Financial terms of the transaction have not been disclosed. Muller, founded in 1918 and headquartered in Dordrecht, will continue operating as an independent unit under the name Boluda Muller Towage, retaining its existing management team and focusing on offshore towage and marine projects worldwide. Former chief executive and owner Bram Muller will remain involved as an adviser, along with the company’s advisory board, as the business transitions to its new ownership. The Dutch operator has built a sizeable presence in the North Sea and Baltic markets, supporting offshore energy and infrastructure projects ranging from transporting wind turbine foundations and offshore substations to heavy lifting and coastal towage. Its fleet includes the 120-tonne bollard pull En Avant 30 and the 90-tonne bollard pull En Avant 25 and En Avant 26 , which can operate both offshore and in ports. Boluda Towage executive chairman Vicente Boluda Ceballos said the acquisition would broaden the group’s specialist offshore capabilities while allowing Muller to continue developing its operations alongside Boluda’s existing European business. The Muller family said joining the Spanish group would provide additional financial capacity for investment, fleet expansion and recruitment in an increasingly capital-intensive offshore market. The takeover marks another step in Boluda’s acquisition drive. Last October, the group struck a $640m deal to acquire Boskalis’ harbour towage and salvage operations in Australia and Papua New Guinea, expanding its reach to more than 230 ports across five continents. The latest transaction also follows last week’s agreement by sister company Boluda Shipping to acquire Dutch multimodal operator Samskip, creating a shortsea network spanning 32 vessels and 18 routes across 28 countries. That deal is expected to close in January 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. articles.body: Europe Tankers Hunter’s VLCC charter dispute balloons to $86m Adis Ajdin November 9, 2026 0 243 1 minute read Hunter Group Hunter Group Norwegian shipping investment company Hunter Group’s long-running dispute with a VLCC charter counterparty has escalated further, with unpaid hire now exceeding $86m after the largest monthly shortfall reported since the row began. The Oslo-listed company disclosed on Monday that its counterparty paid approximately $18.62m less than the amount due for October, marking the eighth consecutive month of reduced payments. The latest shortfall takes the total disputed balance to $86.41m, excluding accrued interest, up from $67.79m at the end of September. Hunter recorded net time charter earnings of approximately $82.89m for October, of which $18.62m remains outstanding. The charterer continues to challenge its obligation to pay the full contractual hire. Hunter maintains that the reductions constitute a breach of contract and said it would continue taking steps to recover the outstanding amounts. The dispute has been running since March and moved into arbitration in London in June, when Hunter initiated proceedings before the London Maritime Arbitrators Association (LMAA) after unpaid hire reached about $28.2m. Hunter’s tanker exposure is centred on two scrubber-fitted VLCCs chartered in at fixed rates and chartered out on floating-rate arrangements linked to the Baltic Exchange’s TD3C benchmark. The structure has given the company exposure to strong crude tanker earnings, but the disagreement with one counterparty has continued to grow alongside the market’s rally. Hunter appointed Erik Mathiesen as permanent chief executive from October 1, with a mandate to oversee the company’s current chartering operations and develop its next phase as the existing VLCC arrangements approach expiry. articles.summary: Container News participated as an official Media Partner in the international maritime conference “Shipping at the Historic Turning Point of 2030”, organised by SK Congress on 5 November 2026 at the InterContinental Athens. The event brought together shipping executives, industry professionals, institutional...
articles.body: Container News participated as an official Media Partner in the international maritime conference “Shipping at the Historic Turning Point of 2030”, organised by SK Congress on 5 November 2026 at the InterContinental Athens. The event brought together shipping executives, industry professionals, institutional representatives and experts to discuss the challenges and developments shaping the future of global shipping, with particular emphasis on maritime leadership, port infrastructure, alternative fuels, geopolitical developments and emerging technologies. The conference opened with a welcome address by Sotiria Katsimicha, President of SK Congress, followed by institutional greetings and a series of thematic discussions involving representatives from across the maritime industry. Industry discussions and key themes The conference programme featured four main panel discussions, beginning with international maritime leadership. Speakers included representatives from Tsavliris Group, Bright Navigation, Minoan Lines and Vernicos Yachts, reflecting different segments of the shipping industry. A second panel focused on ports, shipyards and marinas, bringing together representatives from the Port of Volos, the Greek Marinas Association, Celestyal and CrediaBank. Geopolitical developments and their implications for global shipping were also addressed through a dedicated presentation by Dimitris Abatzidis, Maritime Risk and Compliance Manager at MarineTraffic Operations. The industry’s energy transition formed another central theme, with a panel examining alternative fuels and green infrastructure. Representatives from J.H.I. Steamship, Bunker Holding, the Hellenic Shipbrokers Association and Investment & Finance Ltd were included in the discussion. The final panel explored artificial intelligence and automation, featuring participants from Venergy, BCA College, Xplisi Technologies and the University of the Aegean. The programme also included a presentation on the next era of space technology by renowned space scientist Stamatis Krimigis. Container News participation (From left to right): Alexandros Itimoudis-Geopolitical Analyst, Antonia Saratsopoulou- Managing Editor, Giannis Nikolakis- Managing Director Container News was represented at the conference by Giannis Nikolakis, Managing Director, Antonia Saratsopoulou, Managing Editor, and Alexandros Itimoudis, Geopolitical Analyst. As an official Media Partner, Container News supported the initiative, which provided an opportunity for industry professionals to exchange perspectives, strengthen connections and explore developments affecting the maritime sector. The conference concluded with a networking reception, bringing together representatives from shipping companies, ports, shipyards, energy and technology businesses, alongside institutional and diplomatic participants.

articles.summary: Russia has taken control of two modern heavy-lift carriers previously involved in transporting equipment for the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project, adding specialized project cargo vessels to an expanding network of shipping assets supporting the country's Arctic energy ambitions.

(Source: Supplied) Russia has taken control of two modern heavy-lift carriers previously involved in transporting equipment for the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project , adding specialized project cargo vessels to an expanding network of shipping assets supporting the country’s Arctic energy ambitions. The ownership change gives Moscow greater control over a critical part of the supply chain for its Arctic energy projects, from transporting construction modules to remote project sites to potentially delivering finished LNG infrastructure to future overseas customers. It also illustrates how Russia’s shadow fleet is evolving beyond the transportation of sanctioned oil and LNG into a more comprehensive logistics network supporting the entire lifecycle of its energy projects. The vessels, Bright (IMO 9830769) and Glory (IMO 9934498), have reappeared on the Automatic Identification System (AIS) near Murmansk under the Russian flag, following changes in ownership and management to Russia’s Eco Shipping LLC, according to vessel records reviewed by gCaptain. Equasis identifies Guangdong Nan Feng Shipping Co. as their previous owner. No information about the sale, its timing or financial terms has been made public. Neither vessel currently appears in the fleet listing on Eco Shipping’s website, although Equasis confirms the ownership changes. The two vessels have a history of transporting oversized equipment for Arctic LNG 2. Glory previously sailed as Nan Feng Zhi Xing and Glory Ocean , while Bright has also operated under the names Zhi Xian Zhi Xing , Hunter Star and Bright Ocean . Both have been involved in transporting LNG project modules from China to Russia . Earlier this year, the carriers delivered modules intended for the project’s third production train to Novatek’s LNG construction center at Belokamenka near Murmansk. In September, they returned to China and loaded two additional onshore power-generation (OPP) modules intended for the project’s second train. The subsequent voyage to Arctic LNG 2 was conducted largely outside public tracking. The vessels switched off their AIS transponders while sailing north across the Pacific toward the Bering Strait in mid-September. They eventually delivered the modules to the Utrenniy terminal serving Arctic LNG 2 without broadcasting their positions. Both ships have since reappeared on AIS near Murmansk under their new Russian registration. The future deployment of Bright and Glory remains unclear. At least seven additional modules intended for Arctic LNG 2’s third train remain in China, according to satellite imagery, with some appearing complete and others still under construction. The two carriers could potentially return to China to collect additional equipment. Their new ownership could also open the door to other assignments supporting Russian LNG ambitions. Novatek has expressed interest in exporting its LNG technology and offshore platform concepts to international markets, including Africa and potentially Alaska . Heavy-lift carriers under Russian control could eventually transport modules from Belokamenka or other Russian facilities to overseas customers, rather than relying on foreign-owned vessels for such deliveries. The development comes as two other Chinese heavy-lift carriers with connections to Russian Arctic shipping have attracted attention off Norway’s northern coast near Andøya . One of them, Ya Qing Hai Yang , formerly known as Ocean 28 , delivered a substation module from China to Arctic LNG 2 in 2024. The vessel, which encountered difficulties navigating ice-covered waters in the Chukchi Sea requiring assistance from Russian icebreakers and tugs, is sanctioned by the United States, European Union and United Kingdom. The second vessel, Jian Yang Cheng He , has also been involved in voyages along the Northern Sea Route and has attracted scrutiny from Norwegian authorities. Norwegian authorities inspected both vessels after they appeared off the coast, with Ya Qing Hai Yang subsequently detained over deficiencies including an invalid flag registration and missing certificates. The developments highlight how Russia’s shadow fleet is expanding beyond conventional oil tankers and LNG carriers. By bringing specialized heavy-lift vessels under domestic ownership and management, Moscow is gaining greater control over the transportation infrastructure required to sustain its Arctic energy projects, while reducing reliance on foreign-owned shipping companies. The use of AIS-dark voyages has become a recurring feature of this trade, making independent monitoring of vessel movements and cargo deliveries considerably more difficult. Switching off AIS while navigating the Arctic is particularly concerning given the region’s remote operating environment and the importance of reliable vessel tracking for maritime safety. Transparency surrounding Northern Sea Route operations has also deteriorated in recent years. Russian authorities no longer publish the daily operational shipping logs previously used to monitor traffic and have stopped making permit applications and granted permits publicly available. articles.title: SSE secures grid connection consent for third phase of 4.1 GW offshore wind project
articles.summary: SSE Renewables has secured a marine licence from the UK’s Marine Management Organisation (MMO) for the export cable infrastructure of its Berwick...
articles.body: Authorities & Government November 9, 2026 · 1 minute ago SSE secures grid connection consent for third phase of 4.1 GW offshore wind project AB Adrijana Buljan Offshore Wind 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email SSE SSE Renewables has secured a marine licence from the UK’s Marine Management Organisation (MMO) for the export cable infrastructure of its Berwick Bank C offshore wind farm in English waters, completing the required consents for the project's grid connection. Known as the Cambois Connection, the infrastructure will link the offshore wind farm to the national transmission network at Cambois, near Blyth in Northumberland. The approved scheme includes up to four high-voltage direct current (HVDC) export cables, with transmission capacity of up to 1.8 GW. The MMO’s decision follows the consent granted by the Scottish government in July 2025 for the three-phase, 4.1 GW Berwick Bank in Scottish waters. Northumberland County Council approved the onshore transmission infrastructure in November 2024, including the export cable landfall, converter station and associated grid connections. SSE Berwick Bank C is the third phase of SSE’s Berwick Bank offshore wind project, located in the outer Firth of Forth, approximately 38 kilometers east of the Scottish Borders coast. The wider development is planned across three phases of roughly equal size and could generate enough electricity to supply more than six million UK homes annually if fully built. The Berwick Bank project has two grid connection points, one at Branxton in East Lothian and one in Blyth. The export cables connecting to Branxton received the Scottish government's consent in July 2025, when the offshore wind project was approved. The latest marine licence completes the required consents for the Cambois connection, which will serve the project's third phase, Berwick Bank C. articles.body: Hai An is preparing to take over the 2,702 TEU container vessel Green View before deploying the ship on a regional service connecting Vietnam, China and Thailand. A team of 19 officers and crew members is scheduled to travel from Hai Phong to Ho Chi Minh City on 9 November. The team will board the vessel on 10 November and begin the formal takeover and operational familiarisation process. The handover will take place at the anchorage area of Cat Lai Port in Ho Chi Minh City. Crew completes safety training Ahead of the takeover, Hai An Maritime Management and Hai An Container Transport organised a pre-boarding safety programme for the assigned crew on 6 November. The training covered maritime safety, risk prevention, emergency response procedures and compliance with operational requirements. Crew members were also briefed on inspecting the vessel’s machinery, equipment and technical documentation. Once aboard, the team will familiarise itself with the vessel’s systems and operating procedures. It will also identify any technical defects requiring repair before Green View enters commercial service. Hai An said the crew will review the ship’s classification certificates and other statutory documents to confirm that it meets the applicable requirements. Green View set for regional deployment Tran Van Quyen, Director of Hai An Container Transport, discussed the takeover plan with the crew before their departure. He also outlined plans to deploy Green View on Hai An’s Vietnam–China–Thailand service after the handover is completed. The vessel takeover forms part of Hai An’s wider fleet development strategy. The Vietnamese carrier is expanding its fleet through a combination of vessel acquisitions and newbuilding projects in China. Hai An recently approved an investment in two 1,900 TEU feeder vessels scheduled for delivery in 2029. It also has larger 7,100 TEU ships under construction as it expands its presence across the Intra-Asia market.

articles.title: Readers Speak: Smarter planning leads AI priorities at container terminals
articles.summary: As artificial intelligence becomes an increasingly prominent topic in port technology, the question of where it can deliver the greatest operational value is gaining importance across the container shipping industry. In its latest Readers Speak poll, Container News asked readers: “Where can AI make the biggest...
articles.body: As artificial intelligence becomes an increasingly prominent topic in port technology, the question of where it can deliver the greatest operational value is gaining importance across the container shipping industry. In its latest Readers Speak poll, Container News asked readers: “Where can AI make the biggest difference in container terminals?” The results revealed a clear preference for smarter planning, which emerged as the leading choice ahead of faster cargo handling, predictive maintenance and improved safety. The findings suggest that readers see the greatest potential for AI in supporting the coordination and organisation of terminal operations rather than focusing primarily on individual operational tasks. Smarter planning emerges as the leading priority Smarter planning attracted the strongest support, establishing a clear lead over the other proposed applications of artificial intelligence. The preference suggests that readers recognise the potential value of AI in helping container terminals manage complex operational decisions, including berth allocation, yard planning, equipment deployment and the coordination of cargo movements. These activities are closely interconnected. Decisions made in one part of a terminal can influence operations elsewhere, making effective planning an important factor in overall performance. AI-supported planning tools could help operators analyse operational information, anticipate potential bottlenecks and adjust resource allocation as conditions change. The poll does not establish whether these technologies are already delivering measurable improvements. Rather, it highlights where readers believe AI has the greatest potential to make a difference. Faster cargo handling remains the second priority Faster cargo handling emerged as the second most frequently selected option, indicating that improving the speed of terminal operations remains an important consideration. AI could potentially support cargo handling by improving the coordination of equipment, reducing unnecessary movements and helping operators respond more efficiently to changing workloads. However, the distinction between faster handling and smarter planning is significant. While faster cargo handling focuses on the movement of containers, smarter planning addresses the decisions that determine how those movements are organised. The stronger preference for planning may therefore reflect a belief that improvements in operational coordination can have broader benefits across terminal activities. Predictive maintenance and safety attract less support Predictive maintenance received a smaller share of responses, despite its potential relevance to equipment availability and terminal reliability. AI-based maintenance systems can analyse equipment data to identify patterns associated with developing faults, potentially allowing operators to schedule maintenance before unexpected failures disrupt operations. Improved safety attracted the least support among the four options. This does not necessarily indicate that readers consider safety unimportant. The poll asked respondents to identify the area where AI could make the biggest difference, rather than to rank the overall importance of different terminal functions. Similarly, the relatively limited support for predictive maintenance should not be interpreted as evidence that equipment reliability is a minor operational concern. The results instead suggest that readers see greater potential for AI to influence terminal-wide planning and cargo handling than these more specific applications. How this fits into the broader Readers Speak trend Previous Readers Speak polls have examined the industry’s priorities for shipping investment, port infrastructure, operational resilience and the challenges affecting container shipping networks. The latest findings extend that discussion into the use of artificial intelligence within container terminals. While earlier polls highlighted the importance of physical infrastructure and network performance, this week’s results suggest that readers also recognise the potential value of improving how existing terminal resources are managed. The strong preference for smarter planning is particularly notable because it places decision-making and coordination ahead of individual technological applications. Ultimately, the findings indicate that readers see AI’s greatest opportunity in container terminals not simply as making equipment work faster, but as helping the entire operation work more intelligently.
takeaways: As artificial intelligence becomes an increasingly prominent topic in port technology, the question of where it can deliver the greatest operational value is gaining importance across the container shipping industry.

The findings suggest that readers see the greatest potential for AI in supporting the coordination and organisation of terminal operations rather than focusing primarily on individual operational tasks.
Smarter planning emerges as the leading priority Smarter planning attracted the strongest support, establishing a clear lead over the other proposed applications of artificial intelligence.

articles.summary: CMA CGM has announced new and revised freight surcharges covering several trade routes connecting Asia with Africa, as well as shipments from Canada’s West Coast to the Indian Subcontinent, Middle East Gulf and Red Sea. The adjustments include Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) on selected African routes and a Rate...
articles.body: CMA CGM has announced new and revised freight surcharges covering several trade routes connecting Asia with Africa, as well as shipments from Canada’s West Coast to the Indian Subcontinent, Middle East Gulf and Red Sea. The adjustments include Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) on selected African routes and a Rate Restoration Initiative (RRI03) for shipments originating from western Canada. Implementation dates range from November 10 to December 3, 2026. New surcharges on Asia–Africa routes CMA CGM will introduce a PSS of US$400 per TEU for all cargo shipped from South China to Mozambique, effective November 10, 2026, based on the loading date. The surcharge will remain in effect until further notice. The carrier has also announced a revised PSS of US$500 per TEU for dry and reefer cargo moving from Southeast Asia to West Africa. This adjustment will apply from November 15, 2026, and is specifically applicable to short-term contracts. Additional changes will affect shipments from China to Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, and Mombasa, Kenya. For cargo originating in South China, a PSS of US$400 per TEU will take effect on November 10, 2026. The same amount will apply to shipments from North and Central China beginning November 15, 2026. CMA CGM noted that the surcharge for shipments originating in China will be subject to filing with the Shanghai Shipping Exchange and/or may be included in the ocean freight rate. Rate restoration measures for Canadian exports Separately, CMA CGM will implement a new Rate Restoration Initiative, designated RRI03, for shipments from Canada’s West Coast to destinations in the Indian Subcontinent, Middle East Gulf and Red Sea. The adjustment will take effect on December 3, 2026, and will apply in addition to previously announced Rate Restoration Initiatives. For shipments to the Middle East Gulf and Red Sea, the increase will be US$1,000 per 20-foot container and US$2,000 per 40-foot or 45-foot container. For cargo moving to the Indian Subcontinent, the amounts will be US$600 per 20-foot container and US$1,200 per 40-foot or 45-foot container. Both adjustments cover all cargo types except Open Top and Flat Rack equipment. CMA CGM stated that the announced adjustments are separate from applicable base ocean freight rates. Additional charges, including bunker-related surcharges, terminal handling charges and other local or contingency fees, may also apply. The latest measures follow earlier freight surcharge announcements across several Asia–Africa trade corridors, reflecting further adjustments to CMA CGM’s pricing structure on selected international routes.

By Lucia Kassai, Devika Krishna Kumar, Charles Gorrivan and Archie Hunter Nov 8, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Oil traders are seeking approval from the US government to use some tankers that were sanctioned for their involvement in shipping illicit oil, in an effort to address a vessel crunch and lower prices. At least four companies, including Trafigura Group, Vitol Group, Mercuria Energy Group Ltd., and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. are in discussions with US officials for licenses that would allow them to purchase or lease some ships that are blacklisted by the US government, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The move comes as the Trump administration tries to lower oil prices that spiked after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, triggering the worst supply disruption in history. Freight rates, a major component in the final price of oil, surged to a record in recent weeks amid tanker shortages and the risks of sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. Ships have been forced to take on longer voyages to secure supplies and charterers have been forced to cough up higher insurance fees. Last month, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the administration is working with investors who buy idled sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use the ships to transport non-sanctioned oil. The idea is to convert “ dark tankers to legitimate tankers ,” he said. Treasury officials are reviewing applications and may issue authorizations on a case-by-case basis, rather than a blanket exemption, said the people, asking not to be named discussing private information. The talks cover about 50 of the roughly 1,600 ships currently sanctioned by the US . No decision is final and the timeframe for approvals is unclear, the people added. Representatives for ADNOC, Trafigura, Mercuria and Vitol declined to comment. The applications include supertankers, the oil industry’s largest vessels, able to transport 2 million barrels, some of the people said. The cost to send US oil to Asia in a supertanker climbed to nearly $40 a barrel in early October, up from $5, a year earlier. While rates have since softened, they remain near historical highs, contributing to oil prices that are hovering around $100 a barrel. To be sure, any licenses from the US Treasury or the Office of Foreign Assets Control would only apply to vessels sanctioned by the US. The European Union and the UK have imposed significant restrictions on Russian and Iranian oil, and targeted the so-called “shadow fleet” used to circumvent restrictions on Russian energy exports. It’s also unclear how much the measure would ultimately lower prices. The Trump administration has unleashed a series of measures aimed at lowering soaring energy costs for American consumers, including releasing millions of barrels from emergency reserves and waiving some fuel-related laws. Still, pump prices remain stubbornly elevated and were a major contributing factor to the Republican Party’s staggering losses in the midterm elections this week. The effectiveness at lowering prices will also depend on the profile of the ships rehabilitated. Repurposing tankers that had been previously idled — such as the tanker named Skipper , which has been sitting off the coast of Texas since December — would have a greater impact than just changing the status of vessels operating in the dark fleet, one of the people said. Related Article: U.S. Seizure of Shadow Fleet Tanker ‘Skipper’ Ends Years-Long Sanctions-Evasion Run While most of the sanctioned ships are older than the mainstream fleet, raising concerns about maintenance and safety, they could still be used in short-distance trips such as between the US and the Caribbean or Latin America, freeing newer tankers for long-haul voyages, the person said. The challenge for the Trump administration is to boost shipping capacity and lower oil prices while trying to prevent bad actors from get an influx of cash. As of Nov. 4, there are 1,568 ships hit by US sanctions, including 462 crude oil tankers, according to Treasury data compiled by Bloomberg. Most remain under the radar of enforcement authorities, typically switching off their satellite location signals. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Caroline Brehman By Laura Curtis Nov 7, 2026 (Bloomberg) –The union representing about 250 security workers at the US’s busiest ports agreed to continue negotiations on a new labor contract for two more weeks, their employers said. The latest extension goes through Nov. 20, with additional talks scheduled with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26 scheduled during that period, the Pacific Maritime Association said in a statement. The two sides had already extended a couple of times, initially from Nov. 1 to Nov. 4 , and then to midnight Friday. “PMA remains committed to reaching a fair agreement at the bargaining table that avoids disruption at the nation’s two busiest ports,” it said. The Friday deadline had coincided with the very moment that the Vincent Thomas Bridge — which connects the ports to a major highway — is set to close for repairs for more than a year. Disruptions at the affected terminals could impact roughly 85% of the cargo that moves through the Port of Long Beach and a third of the cargo at the Port of Los Angeles, according to the PMA. The adjacent ports reported record cargo volumes last month and together handle about a third of they country’s seaborne containerized goods. The previous labor contract expired in July 2025, though the PMA, which represents port terminals and ocean carriers, and ILWU Local 26 have been meeting regularly to negotiate with the assistance of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. The situation escalated recently ago after the union authorized a strike. Local 26 members provide security at six container terminals at the Southern California ports. The PMA warned on Oct. 27 that ILWU dockworkers and marine clerks — who have separate labor contracts and are not party to this dispute — were expected to stand with the Local 26 watchmen in the event of a strike.
